title: "Week 6 — What changes when a model starts asking the questions?"

## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">What kind of evidence does an interview produce, and what changes when a model can choose or write the next probe?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 5 generated fixed candidates before participants encountered them. In an adaptive interview, the participant’s answer changes what comes next. The experimental treatment, data-collection instrument and interaction are now entangled.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish interview purposes and survey modes; explain specificity, range, depth and personal context in the focused interview; distinguish speech-to-text, a text interviewer and text-to-speech; compare an assigned protocol with the path a participant actually received; and audit the source and target of every adaptive probe.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Barrie et al. (2026), “AI and Research Methods,” selected §§10.2 and 10.5.** Places adaptive interviewing between generated interventions and tool-augmented data collection. [Download the chapter PDF](../downloads/readings/ai-and-research-methods-barrie-et-al-2026.pdf) · [APSA Preprints record](https://doi.org/10.33774/apsa-2026-h59kk). [@BarrieEtAl2026AIResearchMethods]
- **Merton and Kendall (1946), “The Focused Interview,” *American Journal of Sociology* 51(6): 541–557.** Supplies the foundational criteria used to evaluate what a probe elicits. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/219886). [@MertonKendall1946]
- **Geiecke and Jaravel (2026), “The Rise of AI-Led Interviews in Social Science.”** A large contemporary text-and-voice implementation with explicit validation. [Paper](https://benjamin.geiecke.com/files/ai_interviews.pdf). [@GeieckeJaravel2026]
:::

## Sociological and methodological background

Interviews have never been neutral containers into which respondents deposit attitudes. Merton and Kendall’s focused interview sought detailed responses to a known situation while allowing unanticipated meanings to emerge. Later feminist and reflexive work made power, reciprocity and the interviewer’s social position part of the method. Standardized survey interviewing pursued comparability; CAPI moved administration onto an interviewer’s computer; CASI allowed self-administration; audio-CASI added recorded speech for accessibility and privacy. These modes change what respondents hear, disclose and understand.

An LLM interviewer redistributes familiar decisions. A protocol can set topic boundaries and fixed questions. After an answer, a model can select a prepared follow-up or compose a new one. The second option can pursue specificity, but it can also lead, presuppose a cause, repeat itself or create incomparable paths across participants.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Geiecke and Jaravel use text and voice, so their system includes speech-to-text before the language model and text-to-speech after it. Jack and colleagues use a web chatbot built around Gemini Flash 1.5 and study both the interview data and researchers’ experience of the system. These implementations make privacy, retention and data ownership design questions: which service receives audio, where transcripts are stored, and whether data are reused. A local stack can reduce external transfer, but it demands hardware, model files, maintenance and usually slower inference.

The evaluation target also matters. Completion rate and conversational fluency do not establish qualitative richness. A controlled design can compare fixed questions, dynamic probing and member checking, but the concepts must be defined: a dynamic prober generates a follow-up from the answer; a member checker asks whether the interviewer’s understanding is accurate.

## Summary and preparation for next week

An adaptive interviewer produces different question paths from the same protocol. After the midterm break, Week 7 moves from asking people questions to asking a model to answer as if it were a person.
